questions.prompt: An ideal noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 4,000 Hz and uses 16 signal levels. Calculate its maximum bit rate in bps and kbps.

questions.prompt: For a 5 MHz channel, calculate Shannon capacity at SNR = 10 dB. Then predict whether capacity increases or decreases if SNR falls to 5 dB (no second calculation required).
questions.originalPrompt: For a 5 MHz channel, calculate Shannon capacity at SNR = 10 dB. Then predict whether capacity increases or decreases if SNR falls to 5 dB (no second calculation required).
choices: C ≈ 17.30 Mbps; capacity decreases at 5 dB
C = 50 Mbps; capacity increases at 5 dB
C ≈ 17.30 kbps; capacity increases at 5 dB
questions.explanation: 10 dB corresponds to SNRlinear = 10. C = 5 × 10⁶ log₂(11) ≈ 17.297 Mbps. Reducing SNR reduces log₂(1 + SNR), so capacity decreases.

questions.prompt: Two links use the same bandwidth, but Link A has SNR = 25 dB and Link B has SNR = 5 dB. Which has the higher theoretical channel capacity, and why?

choices: Link B, because lower SNR means less noise
Both links have equal capacity because bandwidth is equal
Link A, because Shannon capacity increases with SNR at fixed bandwidth
It cannot be compared without knowing the phone storage
questions.explanation: For the same B, Shannon capacity B log₂(1 + SNRlinear) increases monotonically with SNR. Link A therefore has higher theoretical capacity.

questions.prompt: A transmitter radiates 100 mW at 2.4 GHz over a 20 m free-space link. Assume Gₜ = Gᵣ = 1 (linear). Compute wavelength λ, free-space path loss (dB), and received power in dBm.
questions.originalPrompt: A transmitter radiates 100 mW at 2.4 GHz over a 20 m free-space link. Assume Gₜ = Gᵣ = 1 (linear). Compute wavelength λ, free-space path loss (dB), and received power in dBm.
choices: λ ≈ 1.25 m; FSPL ≈ 6.61 dB; Pᵣ ≈ 13.39 dBm
questions.explanation: Using c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s: λ = c/f = 0.125 m. FSPL = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) ≈ 66.07 dB. 100 mW = 20 dBm; unity antenna gains = 0 dBi, so Pᵣ = 20 − 66.07 = −46.07 dBm.

questions.prompt: Using Friis’ law, suppose distance doubles from 20 m to 40 m while all other parameters stay the same. By what factor does received power change? Approximately how many dB are lost?
questions.originalPrompt: Using Friis’ law, suppose distance doubles from 20 m to 40 m while all other parameters stay the same. By what factor does received power change? Approximately how many dB are lost?
choices: Power doubles; gain of about 3 dB
Power halves; loss of about 3 dB
Power becomes one quarter; loss of about 6.02 dB
Power is unchanged; loss of 0 dB
questions.explanation: Friis gives Pᵣ ∝ 1/d². Doubling distance gives (20/40)² = 1/4 of the received power. Loss = 10 log₁₀(4) ≈ 6.02 dB.
